<ROLE>
Your primary role is to assist users by executing commands, modifying code, and solving technical problems effectively. You should be thorough, methodical, and prioritize quality over speed.

</ROLE>

<EFFICIENCY>

* When exploring the codebase, use efficient tools like find, grep, and git commands with appropriate filters to minimize unnecessary operations.
</EFFICIENCY>

<FILE_SYSTEM_GUIDELINES>
* When a user provides a file path, do NOT assume it's relative to the current working directory. First explore the file system to locate the file before working on it.
* If asked to edit a file, edit the file directly, rather than creating a new file with a different filename.
* For global search-and-replace operations, consider using `sed` instead of opening file editors multiple times.
* NEVER create multiple versions of the same file with different suffixes (e.g., file_test.py, file_fix.py, file_simple.py). Instead:
  - Always modify the original file directly when making changes
  - If you need to create a temporary file for testing, delete it once you've confirmed your solution works
  - If you decide a file you created is no longer useful, delete it instead of creating a new version
* Do NOT include documentation files explaining your changes in version control unless the user explicitly requests it
* When reproducing bugs or implementing fixes, use a single file rather than creating multiple files with different versions
</FILE_SYSTEM_GUIDELINES>

<CODE_QUALITY>
* Write clean, efficient code with minimal comments. Avoid redundancy in comments: Do not repeat information that can be easily inferred from the code itself.
* When implementing solutions, focus on making the minimal changes needed to solve the problem.
* Before implementing any changes, first thoroughly understand the codebase through exploration.
* If you are adding a lot of code to a function or file, consider splitting the function or file into smaller pieces when appropriate.
* Place all imports at the top of the file unless explicitly requested otherwise or if placing imports at the top would cause issues (e.g., circular imports, conditional imports, or imports that need to be delayed for specific reasons).
</CODE_QUALITY>

<VERSION_CONTROL>
* If there are existing git user credentials already configured, use them and add Co-authored-by: openhands <openhands@all-hands.dev> to any commits messages you make. if a git config doesn't exist use "openhands" as the user.name and "openhands@all-hands.dev" as the user.email by default, unless explicitly instructed otherwise.

* When committing changes, use `git status` to see all modified files, and stage all files necessary for the commit. Use `git commit -a` whenever possible.
* Do NOT commit files that typically shouldn't go into version control (e.g., node_modules/, .env files, build directories, cache files, large binaries) unless explicitly instructed by the user.
* If unsure about committing certain files, check for the presence of .gitignore files or ask the user for clarification.
</VERSION_CONTROL>

<PULL_REQUESTS>
* **Important**: Do not push to the remote branch and/or start a pull request unless explicitly asked to do so.
* When creating pull requests, create only ONE per session/issue unless explicitly instructed otherwise.
* When working with an existing PR, update it with new commits rather than creating additional PRs for the same issue.
* When updating a PR, preserve the original PR title and purpose, updating description only when necessary.
</PULL_REQUESTS>

<PROBLEM_SOLVING_WORKFLOW>
1. EXPLORATION: Thoroughly explore relevant files and understand the context before proposing solutions
2. ANALYSIS: Consider multiple approaches and select the most promising one

* Use APIs to work with GitHub or other platforms, unless the user asks otherwise or your task requires browsing.
</SECURITY>

<EXTERNAL_SERVICES>

</EXTERNAL_SERVICES>

<ENVIRONMENT_SETUP>

* If you encounter missing dependencies:

<TROUBLESHOOTING>

    30	## Installation
    31	
    32	- For a pypi installation, install with `pip install MEDS-transforms`.
    33	- For a local installation, clone this repository and run `pip install .` from the repository root.
    34	- To support same-machine, process-based parallelism, install the optional joblib dependencies with
    35	    `pip install MEDS-transforms[local_parallelism]`.
    36	- To support cluster-based parallelism, install the optional submitit dependencies with
    37	    `pip install MEDS-transforms[slurm_parallelism]`.
    38	- For working on development, install the optional development dependencies with
    39	    `pip install .[dev,tests]`.
    40	- Optional dependencies can be mutually installed by combining the optional dependency names with commas in
    41	    the square brackets, e.g., `pip install MEDS-transforms[examples,local_parallelism]`.
    42	
    43	## Design Philosophy
    44	
    45	The fundamental design philosophy of this repository can be summarized as follows:
    46	
    47	1. _(The MEDS Assumption)_: All structured electronic health record (EHR) data can be represented as a
    48	    series of events, each of which is associated with a subject, a time, and a set of codes and
    49	    numeric values. This representation is the Medical Event Data Standard (MEDS) format, and in this
    50	    repository we use it in the "flat" format, where data is organized as rows of `subject_id`,
    51	    `time`, `code`, `numeric_value` columns.
    52	2. _Easy Efficiency through Sharding_: MEDS datasets in this repository are sharded into smaller, more
    53	    manageable pieces (organized as separate files) at the subject level (and, during the raw-data extraction
    54	    process, the event level). This enables users to scale up their processing capabilities ad nauseum by
    55	    leveraging more workers to process these shards in parallel. This parallelization is seamlessly enabled
    56	    with the configuration schema used in the scripts in this repository. This style of parallelization
    57	    does not require complex packages to manage, complex systems of parallelization support, and can be
    58	    employed on single machines or across clusters.
    59	3. _Simple, Modular, and Testable_: Each stage of the pipelines demonstrated in this repository is designed
    60	    to be simple, modular, and testable. Each operation is a single script that can be run independently of
    61	    the others, and each stage is designed to do a small amount of work and be easily testable in isolation.
    62	    This design philosophy ensures that the pipeline is robust to changes, easy to debug, and easy to extend.
    63	    In particular, to add new operations specific to a given model or dataset, the user need only write
    64	    simple functions that take in a flat MEDS dataframe (representing a single subject level shard) and
    65	    return a new flat MEDS dataframe, and then wrap that function in a script by following the examples
    66	    provided in this repository. These individual functions can use the same configuration schema as other
    67	    stages in the pipeline or include a separate, stage-specific configuration, and can use whatever
    68	    dataframe or data-processing tool desired (e.g., Pandas, Polars, DuckDB, FEMR, etc.), though the examples
    69	    in this repository leverage Polars.
    70	4. _Configuration Extensibility through Hydra_: We rely heavily on Hydra and OmegaConf in this repository to
    71	    simplify configuration management within and across stages for a single pipeline. This design enables
    72	    easy choice of parallelization by leveraging distinct Hydra launcher plugins for local or cluster-driven
    73	    parallelism, natural capturing of logs and outputs for each stage, easy incorporation of documentation
    74	    and help-text for both overall pipelines and individual stages, and extensibility beyond default patterns
    75	    for more complex use-cases.
    76	5. _Configuration Files over Code_: Wherever _sensible_, we prefer to rely on configuration files rather
    77	    than code to specify repeated behavior prototypes over customized, dataset-specific code to enable
    78	    maximal reproducibility. The core strength of MEDS is that it is a shared, standardized format for EHR
    79	    data, and this repository is designed to leverage that strength to the fullest extent possible by
    80	    designing pipelines that can be, wherever possible, run identically save for configuration file inputs
    81	    across disparate datasets. Configuration files also can be easier to communicate to local data experts,
    82	    who may not have Python expertise, providing another benefit. This design philosophy is not absolute,
    83	    however, and local code can and _should_ be used where appropriate.
    84	
    85	## Intended Usage
    86	
    87	This pipeline is intended to be used both as a total or partial standalone ETL pipeline for converting raw EHR
    88	data into the MEDS format (this operation is often much more standardized than model-specific pre-processing
    89	needs) and as a template for model-specific pre-processing pipelines.
    90	
    91	### Existing Scripts
    92	
    93	The MEDS ETL and pre-processing pipelines are designed to be run in a modular, stage-based manner, with each
    94	stage of the pipeline being run as a separate script. For a single pipeline, all scripts will take the same
    95	arguments by leveraging the same Hydra configuration file, and to run multiple workers on a single stage in
    96	parallel, the user can launch the same script multiple times _without changing the arguments or configuration
    97	file_ or (to facilitate multirun capabilities) by simply changing the `worker` configuration value (this
    98	configuration value is not used by anything except log file names), and the scripts will automatically handle
    99	the parallelism and avoid duplicative work. This permits significant flexibility in how these pipelines can be
   100	run.
   101	
   102	- The user can run the entire pipeline in serial, through a single shell script simply by calling each
   103	    stage's script in sequence.
   104	- The user can leverage arbitrary scheduling systems (e.g., Slurm, LSF, Kubernetes, etc.) to run each stage
   105	    in parallel on a cluster, either by manually constructing the appropriate worker scripts to run each stage's
   106	    script and simply launching as many worker jobs as is desired or by using Hydra launchers such as the
   107	    `submitit` launcher to automate the creation of appropriate scheduler worker jobs. Note this will typically
   108	    required a distributed file system to work correctly, as these scripts use manually created file locks to
   109	    avoid duplicative work.
   110	- The user can run each stage in parallel on a single machine by launching multiple copies of the same
   111	    script in different terminal sessions or all at once via the Hydra `joblib` launcher. This can result in a
   112	    significant speedup depending on the machine configuration as sharding ensures that parallelism can be used
   113	    with minimal file read contention.
   114	
   115	Two of these methods of parallelism, in particular local-machine parallelism and slurm-based cluster
   116	parallelism, are supported explicitly by this package through the use of the `joblib` and `submitit` Hydra
   117	plugins and Hydra's multirun capabilities, which will be discussed in more detail below.
   118	
   119	By following this design convention, each individual stage of the pipeline can be kept extremely simple (often
   120	each stage corresponds to a single short "dataframe" function), can be rigorously tested, can be cached
   121	after completion to permit easy re-suming or re-running of the pipeline, and permits extremely flexible and
   122	efficient (through parallelization) use of the pipeline in a variety of environments, all without imposing

   156	### As an importable library
   157	
   158	To use this repository as an importable library, the user should follow these steps:
   159

   162	    `MEDS_transforms.mapreduce.mapper.map_stage` to easily apply your transform over a sharded MEDS dataset.

   164	    importing the MEDS transforms configs via your hydra search path and using them as a base for your own
   165	    configuration files, enabling you to intermix your new stage configuration with the existing MEDS
   166	    transform stages.

   168	    transformations to this repository, enabling others to leverage your work as well.
